description:
Ra-Thermal Labs is an AI & software engineering team building FIRMS-Harmony to unify 26 years of NASA MODIS (1km) & VIIRS (375m) fire records into a calibrated 2000-2026 Burn Activity Calendar.

Our Stack: Python, Polars, Uber H3 spatial indexing, LightGBM, PyTorch, OpenCV, FastAPI & React. With our core harmonization pipeline ready, we are building to win Global Nominee.
summary:
Ra-Thermal developed Delta Fire Calendar, an interactive web application addressing the “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” challenge.

Using NASA FIRMS records spanning November 2000 to December 2025, our application explores satellite-detected thermal activity within a defined Nile Delta study area. It combines a monthly calendar, historical median comparisons, cross-sensor calibration, detection-disagreement mapping, and CSV exports.

The project addresses a key interpretation problem: changes in detection counts can reflect differences between satellite sensors as well as changes in thermal activity. Our workflow preserves source information and distinguishes directly observed records from calibrated estimates.

Researchers can examine seasonal patterns, investigate unusual months, and identify cases requiring further review. By making the assumptions and limitations of historical comparisons visible, Delta Fire Calendar supports more transparent environmental analysis.
details:
WHAT WE BUILT

Delta Fire Calendar is an interactive application for exploring historical satellite-detected thermal activity in Egypt’s Nile Delta. Our primary intended users are environmental researchers and analysts investigating seasonal patterns and preparing monitoring reports.

The application helps users examine a central question: how much of an apparent change in detections reflects thermal activity, and how much may reflect differences between observation systems?

HOW IT WORKS

Our Python pipeline processes historical MODIS and VIIRS active-fire and thermal-anomaly records distributed through NASA FIRMS.

The study rectangle extends from 29.8° to 31.65°N and 29.5° to 32.5°E. It is an analytical area of interest, not an administrative boundary.

The pipeline filters records to this region, retains satellite and source information, and organizes detections into monthly summaries and a 0.25° spatial grid. The current historical dataset spans November 2000 through December 2025, with different periods of availability for each satellite.

Cross-sensor calibration estimates a common S-NPP reference scale where supported by validation. We distinguish calibrated estimates from directly observed values and retain unsuccessful calibration results rather than presenting every adjustment as an improvement. S-NPP serves as a reference sensor, not ground truth.

MAIN FEATURES

• An interactive calendar for exploring monthly detection patterns.
• Historical median comparisons for investigating selected months.
• A map showing detections recorded by S-NPP only, Aqua only, or both within the same grid cell and day.
• Visibility into the contribution of observed and reconstructed records to historical comparisons.
• CSV exports for further analysis and reproducibility.

INTENDED BENEFITS

The project supports the investigation of seasonal thermal activity and helps analysts identify patterns requiring closer review.

Its intended value is more transparent historical comparison: users can examine the records and assumptions behind a result before interpreting an apparent increase or decrease.

The Nile Delta is a relevant setting for studying activity that may include agricultural burning. However, satellite detections alone do not establish the burning source, quantify emissions, or demonstrate a contribution to a particular air-pollution event.

TOOLS AND IMPLEMENTATION

We used Python for data processing, aggregation, calibration, and validation. The interface uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG-based grid visualization. CSV files support data exchange and downloadable results.

NASA FIRMS provides the observational data used in the historical analysis.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

Our approach connects a localized historical calendar with calibration evidence, source traceability, and cross-sensor disagreement.

We considered differences in sensor resolution, observation timing, processing versions, data availability, and the interpretation of reconstructed historical values. The interface is designed to make these limitations understandable alongside the results.

CURRENT LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Detection disagreement does not prove that one sensor missed the same fire seen by another. A complete downloaded interval also does not establish clear-sky observation coverage.

Fire-mask and geolocation data are being acquired for an October 2023 case study. Planned improvements include coverage analysis and a month-interpretation card comparing detection count, summed observed fire radiative power, and detected cell-days against suitable historical references.

These additions will be presented as completed features only after integration and testing. Independent validation remains necessary for stronger claims about confirmed fires or agricultural burning.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE

ChatGPT was used for project ideation, drafting explanatory text, coding assistance, debugging guidance, and discussion of analytical methods and results. The underlying NASA satellite observations were not generated by AI.
